newsitem.title: USA: U.S. GDP seen giving impetus to Fed for rate hike.
newsitem.headline: U.S. GDP seen giving impetus to Fed for rate hike.

text.p: The red hot U.S. economy grew at a surprisingly robust 5.6 percent annualized pace in the first quarter, providing the Federal Reserve with further justification to tighten credit again this year, experts said.
"With a growth number like that, they would probably act again to moderate it by tightening at least once more," said Carol Stone, a senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
The rise in first-quarter U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was well above the expected 4.1-percent increase.
The 5.6-percent first quarter GDP rise was the largest since a 6.0-percent gain in the fourth quarter of 1987.
Consumers went on a shopping spree in the first quarter as spending surged 6.4 percent. This rise in consumer outlays was the largest since a 7.2 percent increase in the first quarter of 1988.
The strong data prompted some economists to wonder whether the Fed may hike rates by more than 25 basis points.
"Earlier, most of us thought maybe a quarter point (hike) on May 20 was likely," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
"Now I'm not sure," Sohn said. "(The Fed may) decide to go for a half-point hike in interest rates."
Fed policymakers increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, the first tightening in more than two years. Their next meeting is slated for May 20.
Although analysts agreed the GDP reports showed surprising strength, they also pointed out certain aspects of the report may signal slower economic growth in the future.
Specifically, they cited the whopping $46.1 billion rise in business inventories in the first quarter.

"The inventory story is relevant because if the inventory numbers are right, that means that they were probably building (inventories) at the correct pace and that means that they wouldn't have to build more inventories going forward," said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.
On the other hand, Tainer said, if the report overestimated inventory building, that means businesses will continue to accumulate inventories going forward.
"And that sets up the second quarter for healthy (GDP) growth as well," she added.
The Commerce Department report released on Wednesday is the initial estimate of first quarter economic growth. The numbers are subject to revision in subsequent reports.
Sohn warned, "Right now, the concern is the economy is growing too fast. Later on, my concern is the economy may slow fairly dramatically."
Some economists were encouraged by the picture painted by Wednesday's GDP report and Tuesday's report on the Employment Cost Index, which showed a weaker-than-expected 0.6-percent gain.
"It's a wonderful combination of information," Stone said. "It (says) the economy was tremendously strong in the first quarter, but labor cost remained low."
